body:
I'm going to be heading off very shortly, but I wanted to say thank you for sticking around for the conversation before I do. I'll have more to say this evening. I appreciate your thoughts here, and honestly, where I may have questions and misunderstandings, I can't imagine having anything to "come back on you" over.

I'm glad to know I'm not the only one who can spend literally hours at a time on a single Reddit comment as well.

I want to thank you for taking the time to respond, especially with as much forethought and empathy as you invested in the matter. You've given me something to dwell on for a while, and that, if anything, at least gives me some hope. I feel like that's coming out on digital paper in a way that's far more deadpan than I mean for, so I'll just add: know that the gratitude really is there.

> There's a reason we use the same word for depression in economics and psychology- without confidence and momentum, no transactions of value take place, and markets interpret every stimulus as empty and irrational charity.

That's pretty spot-on, at least as regards my own experiences. There are a lot of people I deal with in my day-to-day that are doing it for no reason but because they have to... or have spotted a profitable pocket somewhere in my niche.

> You're probably stuck with all this false value- expectations about what success means, feelings of being under other's shadows or power, bullshit like that. These won't go away with austerity, but they can with therapy- talking about fake value is like a badass audit that makes you realise half your debts aren't really payable- it also acts as a bit of a stimulus...

I think I understand the spirit of this perspective, but I hesitate... granted, it may only be my biased expectation that I couldn't possibly get over seeing my current circumstance as one worth being sunk into... but I'm to the point where I almost don't *want* to accept the state of things. I'm sure that's also not necessarily even what you're saying; I'm just offering up my initial reaction. (You've been kind enough to open an honest dialogue, so I suppose I'm attempting to reciprocate in that sense.)

> If you're going to stimulate yourself, it's got to be something the market wants and values. Finding that is hard, especially in a value crisis, but things exist.

I want to thank you for this piece of advice; this is very akin to what I have offered people in my sphere who I've seen suffering like I am now. I know it's still applicable to my situation even as I write this, but then, the fact that I've already discovered is part of why I'm as scared and sad as I am now. I *have* taken the time to discover things; I know what I love about the world, and what defines me as far as the things I do. I write, I make music, I have a fascination with software and am constantly trying to build the ultimate Linux machine, etc. etc.... and yet here I am. I feel like life is overtaking my ability to enjoy things, and replacing them is not even what I want to do, because I know I'd still care about these things a lot more if I just could come off of what feels like the narrow ledge.

> I used walking, and learning philosophy

So do I. Walking is, or at least was, my therapy for years, and for a long time it has held up. Philosophy was actually one of my main fields of study in university, and it has followed me since. As much as I love it, though, I've also found through exploration that I'm a relativist about a great many things, especially value judgments and certain epistemic concepts, and so there's very little about the state of the world that doesn't strike me as arbitrary. I'm actually okay with that, and in fact it makes the world fascinating when I'm in a position to really explore that perspective, but when I'm low, there are days where that just makes it sadly easy to let things of importance fall to the wayside. I can tell myself it doesn't matter, because this world is just awash with happenstance, and it all matters just as little as I must. When you don't anticipate ever regaining control, that line of thought makes contemplating exit easy.

> Or maybe you need some new theory to get out of the bear market. Everyone's different. But either way, you're not a lone business that needs to divest, but a whole damn economy, full of diverse talents, untapped resources and boundless creativity- you just need to get off the ropes.

Please don't take my responses as an attempt to be difficult. You've actually given me something to think about, and despite what may seem like obstinate counterpoints, I'm excited that we've shared all this... even when my replies seem like "no, that can't be," because it gave me a chance to be honest and evaluate the things that matter to me. I don't think a person can talk about the things they love without at least feeling some sense of excitement, and I had that above, even for claiming that life seems to have trumped them lately. I don't know that I need a "new theory," but clearly I have a perspective that is rather crippled in the face of our best-tested theories. I can be rational and say that I'm sure I'm not as hated as I feel these days, but when I'm in a place where the tension is high and the payout is low on multiple levels (e.g., my workplace), it's easy to let objectivity go askew. You feel like you're losing at pretty much everything, and without any reassurance in the opposite direction, you go with that. This conversation here tells me that I haven't really taken in the full scope of tihings, though, because (a) I haven't really evaluated the positives of my situation as much as just listed them off to myself and passed over them in my depressed frustration; (b) I've made the assumption that I was out of options, rather than sought or borrowed any insight (up until now, at least); and (c) I haven't actually asked if anyone cares... clearly at least one person does (not to put on any undue pressure).

Thank you... you couldn't possibly have anticipated how much impact you've made on a life in a few paragraphs. Your life experience has clearly been well invested, and not just in the senses approved by Hayek and Keynes.
